questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the second way to use hái introduced in this exchange?
What replaces the completion marker le in the negative of a completed action?
With which negative is the verb yǒu always made negative?
What are the two possible meanings when new-situation le is used with a negative verb?
Write the Chinese for "I don't have any more classes."
In the sentence Méiyou kè le, what is the function of le, and what is méiyou?

answers.answer_text: Le is a new-situation marker, and méiyou is simply the negative of the full verb yǒu.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Is méi(you) ever used together with the completion marker le?

answers.answer_text: No — méi or méiyou replaces the completion marker le; the two are never used together.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Why is the sentence Tā bù lái le ambiguous?

answers.answer_text: Because it can mean either that he was expected to come but changed his mind, or that he used to come at this time but has now stopped.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "He is not my friend anymore."

answers.answer_text: Tā bú shi wǒde péngyou le.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which meaning of hái did you already know?

articles.text:
1. B: Nǐ jīntian hái yǒu kè ma?             Do you have any more classes today?
   A: Méiyou kè le.                         I don't have any more classes.

Notes on No. 1

Hái, "additionally," "also": You have already learned the word hái used as an adverb meaning "still." In this exchange you learn a second way to use hái.

Nǐ hái xiǎng zǒu ma?             Do you still want to leave?
Nǐ hái yào xué shénme?           What else do you want to study?

Méiyou...le: You will remember that in the negative of a completed action, méi or méiyou replaces the completion marker le--is never used together with it.

Tā  |          | lái | le.        (He came.)
Tā  | méi(you) | lái.|            (He did not come.)

In the sentence Méiyou kè le, le is a new-situation marker, and méiyou is simply the negative of the full verb yǒu. (Remember that the verb yǒu is always made negative with méi, never with bù.)

Tā  |      | yǒu kè | le.         (Now he has class. [Due to a change in
                                  the schedule, he now has class at this
                                  time.])
Tā  | méi- | yǒu kè | le.         (He doesn't have any more classes.)

Bù...le/méiyou...le: When the marker le for new situations is used with a negative verb, there are two possible meanings: one is that something that was supposed to happen is now not going to happen; the other is that something that was happening is not happening anymore. Thus the following sentence is ambiguous:

Tā bù lái le.                    He is not coming now. [Either he was
                                 expected to come but changed his mind,
                                 or he used to come at this time but now
                                 has stopped.]

In the context of a conversation, the meaning of the sentence would become clear. Here are more examples with the "anymore" meaning:

Tā bú niàn shū le.               He is not going to study anymore.
                                 [He will no longer attend college.]
Tā bú shi wǒde péngyou le.       He is not my friend anymore.
Méiyou le.                       There is no more.
